doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Pepper Adams, Gil Evans and Johnny Griffin in old age
summary: Pepper Adams hurt by a review, Gil Evans wanting his fair share, Griffin unable to carry his horn; the 22 hours off stage.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Good analogy. So I’m sitting here thinking how to respond to what you just said and I wonder if in all the interviewing that you’ve done, have you ever had a similar situation, who was interviewing someone who is approaching 80 and looking at the world at that time and suggesting a similar attitude. What would you have said to them?

Huh. Well I think about a conversation I had with Gil Evans right at the end of his life, or a conversation I had with Pepper Adams actually is more to the point, also at the end of his life. Pepper was particularly upset about a critical review that John Wilson had written about his performance with Monk and the review was in the New York Times and © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

it was pretty harsh and it really kind of ended Pepper’s opportunity to work with Monk, and he was just downcast thirty years later. The thing with Gil Evans is I don’t know how it came up but what he said in talking about his career, he said, “All I ever wanted was my certified fair share, CFS.” Certified Fair Share. And he said, “I don’t think I ever got it.” I think he’s talking about in terms of credit and in terms of commercial success. And he was really down in the dumps about that too. I don’t know if there is anything I could have said to either one of them other than just hear that it’s more and more difficult to maintain that foxhole humor as you get older. And you know it’s the physical challenges of playing the gig become more difficult than playing the gig. Johnny Griffin at the end, I was with him in France and he said he wasn’t playing gigs anymore. And he was vibrant. We were having lunch and I said, “Why don’t you play gigs anymore?” And he said, “I can’t carry my horn. I can’t physically walk through an airport and carry my horn.” Oh my God, right? People don’t think about how much of this music is physical and a reflection of the 22 hours of the day where you’re not performing. You know the two hours that you get to be on stage with friends is wonderful, but the other 22 hours is brutal.
Yes. Phil Woods said that. He said the stage is the sacred place. It’s everything else that people don’t know about.
